clue.text: Guilt-ridden mole scurrying into fishy dive frequently

indicators.note: '-ridden' means filled with, so the word guilt is stuffed with the next piece
into places the scrambled creature inside the word guilt

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a scurrying mole runs about, so its letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A conscience-stricken mole scampers off into the water.
explanation.walkthrough: '-ridden' (filled with) and 'into' both signal the insertion; 'scurrying' scrambles the burrowing animal. The definition describes a seabird that plunges for its prey.
explanation.definitionFit: This black-and-white seabird feeds by plunging under water after fish again and again.

clue.text: Comes to life again, given what's beneath top dressing?

explanation.surface: Someone revives once they see the underwear beneath the outer clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as UN-DIES, the word reads as the opposite of dying; whole, it is slang for underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Un-dying is reviving, as a coined verb; and underclothes are worn beneath the outer garments.

clue.text: See, it is given feather tails and tarry

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see
the tail end of the word feather is its last two letters

explanation.surface: Look, a bird is sporting tail feathers and dawdling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is given' simply joins the pieces; 'feather tails' supplies the last letters of FEATHER.
explanation.definitionFit: To tarry is to linger or dawdle, the same as hanging about.

clue.text: A card game of which some vestige turns up over East

indicators.note: in a down entry the first piece sits above the second
in a down clue, turning up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a trace is a small remaining sign, some vestige
E is the compass abbreviation for East

explanation.surface: A card game whose faint remains surface over in the East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns up' reverses TRACE into ECART; 'over' puts it above E in the down light.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecarte is a French two-player game played with a short pack of cards.

clue.text: A teak company redesigned a little table offering

indicators.note: something redesigned is put together in a new form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A furniture firm remodels a small teak table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'redesigned' rearranges A, TEAK and CO.
explanation.definitionFit: An oatcake is a small savoury biscuit served at the table.

clue.text: Miss front page over booking top model

indicators.note: in a down entry the first piece is placed above the second

parts.note: a magazine's front page is its cover
a miss is a girl or young woman

explanation.surface: A young woman on the front of a magazine lands a booking as a leading model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' puts COVER above GIRL in the down light; 'booking' only colours the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A cover girl is a fashion model whose photograph fronts a magazine.

clue.text: Plain-spoken, yes, but this isn't'1 an across clue, Ok?

parts.note: a clue that is not across must be a down clue
right is an everyday way of saying okay

explanation.surface: The setter checks, frankly, that this clue runs vertically.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray '1 after isn't is a print smudge; the clue tells the solver it is a down clue and asks for agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: Downright speech is blunt and frank, saying things straight out.

clue.text: Minimum corporal punishment for the junior NCO?

definitions.text: Minimum corporal punishment for the junior NCO?

parts.words: Minimum corporal punishment for the junior NCO?
parts.note: the smallest flogging is a single lash, and a lance corporal wears one chevron on the sleeve

explanation.surface: The least a junior soldier could be flogged.
explanation.walkthrough: A stripe is both a lash from a whip and a chevron of rank; a lance corporal has a single one.
explanation.definitionFit: A lance corporal, the most junior non-commissioned officer, has a single chevron of rank.

clue.text: Clown on an early stage in a swallow-tail

definitions.text: an early stage in a swallow-tail

parts.note: Coco was a famous circus clown

explanation.surface: A clown appears early on in a tailcoat.
explanation.walkthrough: A swallow-tail is a butterfly, not a coat; COCO the Clown was a celebrated British circus performer.
explanation.definitionFit: The silken case of a pupa is a stage the butterfly passes through before emerging.

clue.text: Bosses with sea power

parts.note: the bosses who held command over the navy formed the board running Britain's fleet

explanation.surface: Managers who control the oceans.
explanation.walkthrough: The Admiralty was the British government department that commanded the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: The board of naval chiefs who ran the Royal Navy and its command of the seas.

clue.text: Poor Alice's let heavenly dwelling

indicators.note: poor here means badly made, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written with its S

explanation.surface: Poor Alice rents out a divine home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' rearranges ALICES and LET; 'dwelling' only colours the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Celestial describes the sky or heaven, as in celestial bodies.

clue.text: More sinister development of broken rule involving GI

indicators.note: a broken rule falls apart, so its letters are rearranged together with the soldier

parts.note: taken as written, a US soldier

explanation.surface: A soldier's lawbreaking takes a darker turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges RULE with GI worked in ('involving').
explanation.definitionFit: Uglier can mean more threatening, as an ugly mood turns nastier.

clue.text: Period of rising temperatures engendered over witches' cauldron?

explanation.surface: Witches brew up a heatwave over their pot.
explanation.walkthrough: A warm spell is a stretch of mild weather; it is also a charm cast by witches over a hot cauldron.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretch of mild weather; and an incantation made over a heated pot.

clue.text: Fearfully friendly type?

parts.note: a member of the Society of Friends who is shaking with fear

explanation.surface: Someone timidly amiable.
explanation.walkthrough: Quakers are the Religious Society of Friends; to quake is to tremble with fear.
explanation.definitionFit: Like a member of the Friends, a religious society, while trembling in fright.

clue.text: She gave Long John a leg

definitions.text: She gave Long John a leg

parts.words: She gave Long John a leg
parts.note: a woman's name doubles as the wooden limb of the one-legged pirate Long John Silver

explanation.surface: A woman handed the pirate a limb.
explanation.walkthrough: Long John Silver in Treasure Island has a wooden leg; a girl's name of three letters is also a wooden leg's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name, short for Margaret, and the wooden stump in a pirate's peg-leg.

clue.text: Play without a direct course

indicators.note: without means the letter is dropped from the word play

explanation.surface: A drama lacking any clear direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes the A from PLAY.
explanation.definitionFit: To steer a regular route, as ferries do between ports, is to follow a set course.

clue.text: Opening a doctor round

indicators.note: the doctor's letters go round the a

parts.note: GP is a general practitioner, a family doctor

explanation.surface: A doctor's practice opening its rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts GP around A.
explanation.definitionFit: A gap is a space or hole, an opening.

clue.text: Where a jog led back to a castle?

definitions.text: Where a jog led back to a castle?

parts.note: a jog is a slow run

indicators.note: back means the word led is written in reverse

explanation.surface: A jogger's route that ended up at a castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses LED into DEL. Arundel is a Sussex town in southern England with a large castle.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sussex town is home to a famous castle, the seat of the Dukes of Norfolk.

clue.text: Gas used to make this conveyance overtake cars

definitions.text: Gas used to make this conveyance overtake cars

parts.words: Gas used to make this conveyance overtake cars
parts.note: a craft filled with lighter-than-air gas rises and travels over the traffic below

explanation.surface: Fuel that lets a vehicle overtake the cars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gas' suggests petrol, but here it is the helium or hydrogen that lifts the craft above the cars.
explanation.definitionFit: A dirigible balloon kept aloft by gas, floating above road traffic.

clue.text: Settle back for common chatter

indicators.note: back means the word for settle is written in reverse

parts.note: to settle a bill is to pay it

explanation.surface: Paying up in return for idle gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses PAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Yap is slang for noisy, idle talk.

clue.text: Single-handed seaman first turns out Pearl's mother in a way

indicators.note: first places the sailor at the front of the solitary piece

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor
single-handed means alone, without help

explanation.surface: A lone sailor turns out to be the mother of Pearl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns out' simply links. 'Pearl's mother' suggests a woman called Pearl, but it is mother-of-pearl, the shell's lining.
explanation.definitionFit: This sea mollusc's shell is lined with nacre, a source of mother-of-pearl.

clue.text: Putting together small journal about family relationship

indicators.note: about means the magazine's letters go around the kin

parts.note: mag is short for magazine, a small word for a journal
kin are one's family relations

explanation.surface: Assembling a small magazine about family ties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting together' looks like a charade signal but is the definition, meaning assembling.
explanation.definitionFit: Making is constructing or assembling something.

clue.text: Dusty playwright?

parts.note: a playwright surname that is also a trade covered in flour dust

explanation.surface: A writer covered in dust.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Miller was an American playwright; a miller grinding flour is dusty, and dusty miller is also a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Miller wrote Death of a Salesman; a flour grinder works in a dusty mill.

clue.text: Part of Scotland largely developed without English

indicators.note: developed means grown into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged
without means the English letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A region of Scotland grown mostly free of English influence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' drops E from LARGELY, leaving LARGLY, and 'developed' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: Argyll is a historic county on the west coast of Scotland.

clue.text: General Assembly rising to finish a list of things to be done

definitions.text: list of things to be done

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising reads the letters upwards

parts.note: the end is the finish

explanation.surface: The assembly stands to complete its order of business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' reverses GA into AG in the down light.
explanation.definitionFit: An agenda is the schedule of business to deal with at a meeting.

clue.text: Some bloomer if fury follows South African vote

indicators.note: follows places the fury after the earlier pieces

parts.note: an X marks a vote on a ballot paper
rage is fury

explanation.surface: A gaffe if anger greets a South African ballot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' suggests a blunder, but here it is a flowering plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A saxifrage is a flowering rock plant, something that blooms.

clue.text: Leave by way of early motorway to time

parts.note: per means by or via
the M1 was Britain's first motorway, written with I for one

explanation.surface: Taking leave via the motorway in good time.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1, London to Leeds, was Britain's first full motorway; the 1 becomes I. Leave here is a noun: permission.
explanation.definitionFit: Leave is official permission, such as a pass to be absent.

clue.text: Taking the bounce out of an opponent in court?

definitions.text: Taking the bounce out of an opponent in court?

parts.words: Taking the bounce out of an opponent in court?
parts.note: in tennis, hitting the ball before it bounces denies the opponent's shot its bounce

explanation.surface: Deflating a rival during a legal case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'court' suggests law, but it is a tennis court, where a ball struck before it lands never bounces.
explanation.definitionFit: Striking the ball in mid-air at the net, before it touches the ground.

clue.text: Some sort of sailor, some sort of rascal

indicators.note: some sort of rascal means a different arrangement of those letters

explanation.surface: A sailor who is a bit of a rogue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some sort of' rearranges RASCAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A lascar was an East Indian seaman serving on European ships.

clue.text: Motor fuel is able to be transported in it

definitions.text: Motor fuel is able to be transported in it

parts.note: petrol is the British word for motor fuel
can means is able

explanation.surface: A container for carrying fuel.
explanation.walkthrough: Petrol is British for gasoline.
explanation.definitionFit: A portable container for carrying spare fuel for a car.
